I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Denver, Colorado, USA at 2026-01-11 01:33 MST (UTC-0700) (2026-01-11T08:33:00Z in UTC), at latitude 39.7392 degrees and longitude -104.9903 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is -64.305 degrees and its azimuth is 51.551 degrees, so it is below the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 3.749 degrees and its azimuth is 113.235 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 43.46 percent illuminated, 82.321 degrees from the Sun, and 401200.6 kilometers away. The sky brightness is night, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes—very likely, provided your southeastern horizon is reasonably unobstructed.

The Moon is only **3.75° above the horizon**, at azimuth **113°** (east-southeast). That is low enough that trees, buildings, terrain, haze, and atmospheric extinction could easily hide it, but the Moon’s **43% illumination** makes it far brighter than ordinary stars. Its angular separation from the Sun is **82°**, so it is a waning crescent/near-quarter-type Moon in a dark sky, not lost in twilight. At roughly **401,000 km**, its distance is normal and doesn’t materially affect naked-eye visibility.

Look toward **east-southeast**, about **four finger-widths above a level horizon**—though because it is so low, start scanning just above rooftops or distant terrain. Give your eyes a few minutes to adapt and avoid nearby lights. If you have a clear horizon, you should be able to spot it; if not, wait until it rises higher, when it will be much easier.
